lessons.title: Position Limits, Kill Switches, and Circuit Breakers for a Live Agent

body.text: A drawdown-penalized reward asks the agent to behave safely. It does not guarantee the agent will, especially in a state it never trained on. This lesson builds guardrails that don't ask, they simply prevent, regardless of what the trained policy decides.

children.text: Chapter 3's drawdown penalty and Chapter 5's distributional shift monitoring are both, in an important sense, soft protections: they shape what the agent is incentivized to do, and they flag when something looks wrong, but neither one physically prevents a bad outcome. A trained policy encountering a genuinely novel state, exactly what the shift monitor exists to catch, has no guarantee of behaving the way its training intended, since training never covered that state. Hard guardrails are a categorically different kind of safety. A circuit breaker in an electrical panel does not ask a circuit to learn not to overload; it physically cuts the current once a threshold is crossed, regardless of what caused the overload. This lesson builds the trading equivalent.
Position Limits: Capping Exposure Regardless of What the Agent Wants

Chapter 3's continuous action space already clips its output to a maximum exposure inside the model's own code. A hard position limit repeats that same check again, independently, at the execution layer, immediately before any order is placed, on the principle that the same code path should never be trusted twice. If a bug, an unusual state, or an unexpected model output ever caused the model's own internal clipping to fail, a second, independently implemented check is what stands between that failure and an oversized live position.

body.caption: This class knows nothing about Q-values, policies, or reward functions, deliberately. It is a completely independent layer that any model's output must pass through before becoming a real order, so a bug or an unexpected value inside the model cannot bypass it.

children.text: Kill Switches: A Human-Reachable Full Stop

A kill switch immediately flattens all positions and halts all new trading until someone deliberately restarts the system, not automatically at the start of the next session the way the circuit breaker below does. It needs to be reachable within seconds by whoever is monitoring the strategy, and it needs both a manual trigger, a human decides something looks wrong and hits stop, and automatic triggers that do not wait for a human to notice at all.

body.caption: Manual vs Automatic Kill Switch Triggers

cells: A human monitoring the dashboard from Chapter 6's next lesson notices behavior that looks wrong, even if no automatic threshold has fired yet, and stops the system on judgment alone
ExecutionGuard's max_daily_loss is crossed, exactly as tested above, halting new trades without waiting for a person to react
The live data pipeline stops updating or returns clearly invalid values; trading on a stale or broken feed is worse than not trading at all
Chapter 5's shift monitor fires on several consecutive live states, a pattern this lesson's next section distinguishes from a single, isolated flag

children.text: Circuit Breakers: Losses That Pause Trading for the Day

A circuit breaker is a temporary pause, not a permanent stop: trading halts for the remainder of the day once a threshold is crossed, then resumes automatically at the next session after ExecutionGuard's reset_for_new_day() runs, without requiring a manual restart. This mirrors, on a strategy level, the market-wide circuit filters NSE and SEBI already apply to the index itself, trading halts triggered at defined index move thresholds during a session. The tested ExecutionGuard class above is exactly this kind of circuit breaker: crossing max_daily_loss halted new trading for the rest of that day, verified to force a flat position regardless of what the model proposed afterward, and a fresh reset_for_new_day() call is what brings it back online the next session.

children.text: Testing These Guardrails Before You Need Them

body.text: A guardrail that has never actually been triggered in a test is a belief that a safety mechanism exists, not a verified one. The same discipline this course has applied to every other component, running the environment, checking the reward formula, testing the shift detector against known cases, applies here: deliberately feed ExecutionGuard a sequence of losses that should cross max_daily_loss, and confirm trading_halted actually becomes True and check_and_clip_position actually returns zero afterward, in a test environment, before ever wiring this into anything connected to a live broker API.

body.title: Choosing Where a Safety Check Belongs
body.scenario: A team has a continuous-action PPO agent, from Chapter 4, whose action space already clips outputs to a maximum position size inside the model's own prediction code. A team member argues the separate ExecutionGuard position check from this lesson is redundant and can be removed to simplify the codebase.
body.prompt: Do you agree the ExecutionGuard check is redundant? What specifically would be lost by removing it?
body.modelAnswer: No, the check is not redundant, even though it duplicates logic already present in the model's own action space clipping. The entire point of a second, independently implemented check is that it does not share a failure mode with the first one: if the model's own clipping logic has a bug, if a future code change accidentally removes or weakens it, or if the model's output somehow bypasses its own action space wrapper due to an integration error, the model-side check silently fails to protect anything. An independent ExecutionGuard check, implemented separately and unaware of the model's internals, still catches an oversized position in exactly that scenario, since it does not depend on the same code being correct. Removing it to simplify the codebase would remove the one thing standing between a bug in the model's own action space and a real, live, oversized position, which is precisely the situation hard guardrails exist for.

body.title: Kill Switch vs Circuit Breaker
body.question: Based on this lesson's definitions, what is the key difference between a kill switch and a circuit breaker as used here?
options: There is no difference; the two terms describe the same mechanism
A kill switch only works automatically, while a circuit breaker only works manually
A circuit breaker pauses trading temporarily and resumes automatically at the next session; a kill switch halts trading until a human deliberately restarts the system
A kill switch is only relevant for continuous action spaces, while a circuit breaker is only relevant for discrete ones
body.explanation: The distinction this lesson draws is about how trading resumes, not about manual versus automatic triggers, since both mechanisms can have automatic triggers. ExecutionGuard's daily loss halt is a circuit breaker: it resumes automatically once reset_for_new_day() runs at the next session. A kill switch is a more serious, indefinite stop that stays halted until a human makes a deliberate decision to bring the system back online.

points: Learned safety, a drawdown-penalized reward or distributional shift monitoring, shapes and flags behavior but does not physically prevent a bad outcome the way a hard guardrail does

A position limit enforced independently at the execution layer, outside the model's own action space clipping, protects against a failure in that model-side logic rather than duplicating a check that is trusted to always work

A kill switch halts trading indefinitely until a human deliberately restarts the system; a circuit breaker pauses trading temporarily and resumes automatically at the next session, mirroring the market-wide circuit filters NSE and SEBI already apply to the index itself

ExecutionGuard's position clipping, daily-loss circuit breaker, forced-flat-while-halted behavior, and reset-for-new-day logic were all individually verified, including the exact boundary case at the loss threshold itself
A guardrail that has never been deliberately tested against the exact scenario it exists to catch is a belief a safety mechanism exists, not a verified one

Every hard guardrail in this lesson exists specifically for the case where learned behavior fails, a novel state, a bug, an unexpected value, which is exactly why it cannot depend on the same logic that might be failing in that moment
